metadata.title: Measuring SDG 4: How PIRLS can help

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This booklet describes how PIRLS 2016 and ePIRLS can be used to monitor SDG 4, but it does not provide the microdata analysis specification (e.g., whether complex survey weights were applied, or which weight variable such as W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT was used). PIRLS is administered using a complex sampling design across participating education systems, and standard PIRLS analyses typically require accounting for stratification and clustering when estimating population-representative statistics. The figures and benchmark-based percentages reported here are presented as policy-relevant summaries rather than as a reproducible ML modeling pipeline, so the booklet does not document replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) or weight application details. For any re-analysis using PIRLS microdata, analysts should apply the official PIRLS sampling weights and replicate weights from the international database to obtain correct standard errors and confidence intervals.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is a policy/monitoring booklet that explains how PIRLS and ePIRLS indicators map to SDG 4 targets and illustrates relationships using benchmark thresholds and descriptive comparisons. It does not report an achievement-score modeling procedure that would require explicit plausible-value (PV) handling, nor does it document a missing-data strategy for an empirical predictive analysis. Therefore, PV handling and missing-data handling are not applicable/undocumented in the sense required for an ML extraction.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The booklet does not define an analytic microdata subsample for an ML model. Instead, it reports PIRLS 2016 (and ePIRLS) descriptive results and benchmark-based indicators for grade 4 reading (and online reading for ePIRLS), sometimes focusing on selected countries/territories (e.g., those where fewer than 90% of students were above the low international benchmark, or those where the below-benchmark percentage exceeded a threshold). It also references cross-round comparisons across PIRLS cycles (2001, 2006, 2011, 2016) for countries/territories where data are available.

data.outcome_summary: This booklet explains how PIRLS 2016 (grade 4 reading) and ePIRLS (online reading for grade 4) can be used to monitor Sustainable Development Goal 4. It maps SDG 4 targets and indicators to PIRLS/ePIRLS outputs such as the share of students above the PIRLS low international benchmark, participation in pre-primary education, home learning environments, and relationships between reading outcomes and factors like early reading activities, books at home, language of instruction, and bullying/sense of belonging. It also illustrates teacher-related SDG 4 indicators using PIRLS questionnaire data on teachers’ formal qualifications and areas of emphasis in teacher education. The document provides descriptive comparisons and benchmark-based summaries across participating education systems (61 systems; 50 countries/territories plus benchmarking entities) and highlights that correlations are not causal. Because it is not an empirical ML study, it does not report model training, PV handling, missing-data procedures, or predictive performance metrics.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a UNESCO/IEA policy booklet describing how PIRLS and ePIRLS can inform SDG 4 monitoring, not a paper that trains or evaluates machine learning models on PIRLS microdata. As a result, there is no analytic ML target/predictor pipeline, no reported total analytic sample size, and no documented PV/missing-data handling for an empirical predictive analysis. The extraction therefore treats the document as an assessment/monitoring framework exposition with descriptive benchmark-based results rather than an ML research design.
